stage_description: The fry stage covers roughly the first 5% of a fish's expected lifespan, so its length depends entirely on the species — a few weeks for a short-lived guppy, but many months for a koi that may live 25 to 30 years. Newly hatched, free-swimming fry grow quickly yet are extremely fragile and highly sensitive to any change in their surroundings, which is why stable, warm, well-filtered water is the single most important factor in helping them survive.
nutrition: Offer tiny, frequent meals of appropriately sized food — infusoria, freshly hatched brine shrimp, or finely powdered fry food — several times a day, giving only what is eaten in a minute or two. Overfeeding quickly fouls the water and is a leading cause of fry loss.
activity: Raise fry in a gentle, stable environment with a sponge filter so they cannot be pulled into the intake, plus fine-leaved plants or other cover for security. Keep them separate from adult fish that may eat them, and hold the temperature steady.
veterinary_check_frequency: Fry are especially intolerant of ammonia and nitrite, so test the water often and perform small, frequent partial water changes with temperature-matched water on an established, cycled filter. If illness or heavy losses appear, consult a vet experienced with aquatic species.
warning_signs: Watch for fry that stop eating, fail to grow, hang at the surface gasping, sink to the bottom, or develop fungus or deformities. A sudden rise in deaths almost always points to a water-quality problem that needs immediate attention.
source_name: PetMD How Long Do Fish Live & Kodama Koi Farm
